title: Six Articles of Faith in Islam: IB Student Guide
summary: Six articles of faith explained for IB World Religions SL, with Arabic terms, Qur'anic references, Sunni and Shi'a views, themes, and exam-ready links.
body_markdown:
The **six articles of faith** are a widely used summary of Islamic belief: faith in God, angels, revealed books, prophets, the Last Day, and divine decree. For IB World Religions SL students, however, remembering that list is only the beginning. Strong analysis explains how the beliefs connect, how Muslims interpret them, and how they answer the course's fundamental questions.


The Arabic word *iman* means faith or belief. The related term *aqidah* refers to creed or firmly held doctrine. These beliefs shape a Muslim understanding of reality, human responsibility, revelation, worship, and life after death. They therefore belong not in an isolated list, but within a connected worldview.


Students beginning the topic can use RevisionDojo's[IB World Religions resources](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions) alongside the dedicated[Islam Study Notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-5-islam/notes) to build that wider context.


### The six articles at a glance


Article of faith Arabic term Central idea


Belief in God *Iman bi-Allah* God is one, unique, sovereign, and worthy of worship


Belief in angels *Iman bil-mala'ikah* Angels are created beings who carry out God's commands


Belief in revealed books *Iman bil-kutub* God has communicated guidance through revelation


Belief in prophets *Iman bil-rusul* God sent human messengers to guide communities


Belief in the Last Day *Iman bil-yawm al-akhir* Human beings will be resurrected and judged


Belief in divine decree *Iman bil-qadar* God's knowledge and sovereignty encompass creation


The Qur'an 4:136 commands belief in God, His angels, His books, His messengers, and the Last Day. The well-known Hadith of Jibril, recorded in *Sahih Muslim* , includes these beliefs and belief in divine decree, both its good and its difficult dimensions. Together, these texts provide the principal basis for the familiar six-part formulation.


Two students compare a small stack of memorised cards with an enormous web of conceptual connections.


### Belief in God: tawhid


*Tawhid* means the oneness and unity of God. It is the foundation of Islamic theology. The Qur'an's Surah al-Ikhlas, 112:1-4, declares that God is one, self-sufficient, neither begetting nor begotten, and without equal.


Tawhid is more than the mathematical claim that only one deity exists. It means that worship belongs to God alone and that nothing in creation shares God's divine status. Associating partners with God is called *shirk* , which Islamic teaching treats as a fundamental theological error.


This belief addresses the IB question **“What is the human condition?”** Humans are created beings, dependent upon God but capable of acknowledging or ignoring divine guidance. It also shapes **ethics and moral conduct** because accountability is grounded in God's authority, mercy, and justice.


### Belief in angels: mala'ikah


Angels, *mala'ikah* , belong to the unseen dimension of existence, known as *al-ghayb* . They are not divine and are not objects of worship. They serve God and perform roles described in the Qur'an and hadith.


Jibril, or Gabriel, communicates revelation. Mikail is traditionally associated with provision, while Israfil is associated with the trumpet announcing resurrection. The Qur'an also describes angels who record human deeds, including in 82:10-12.


For IB analysis, angels connect **doctrines and beliefs** with **religious experience** . Revelation reaches prophets through Jibril, while belief in angels gives ordinary actions a wider spiritual context. A Muslim cannot ordinarily verify angels through the senses, so the doctrine also raises questions about faith, knowledge, and the authority of sacred testimony.


### Belief in revealed books: kutub


Muslims believe that God has provided guidance through revealed scriptures, or *kutub* . These include the *Tawrat* associated with Musa, the *Zabur* associated with Dawud, the *Injil* given to Isa, and the Qur'an revealed to Muhammad. English equivalents include Torah, Psalms, and Gospel, although Islamic understandings of these revelations should not automatically be treated as identical to every present-day biblical collection.


The Qur'an is understood by Muslims as God's final revelation and as confirming earlier revelation. In Islamic belief, its Arabic wording has a distinctive sacred status. Translation can communicate meaning, but it is generally distinguished from the Arabic Qur'an itself.


This article relates directly to the IB theme of **sacred texts** . A strong response can examine composition, interpretation, authority, recitation, and application rather than simply naming four books. RevisionDojo's[introduction to World Religions notes](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-world-religions/ib-world-religions-1-introduction-to-world-religions/notes) can help students apply those analytical categories consistently.


### Belief in prophets and messengers


Prophets are known as *anbiya* , the plural of *nabi* . Messengers are *rusul* , the plural of *rasul* . Muslim scholars have discussed the precise distinction between these categories, but a messenger is commonly understood as one entrusted with a particular divine message for a community.


Islam recognizes figures including Adam, Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, Dawud, Isa, and Muhammad. Muslims regard them as human beings selected by God, not as divine beings. Muhammad is described in Qur'an 33:40 as the “seal of the prophets,” which Muslims understand to mean that prophethood culminates with him.


Prophethood helps answer **“How do we get there?”** Divine guidance is not left as an abstraction. It is communicated and embodied through human messengers. Their examples also connect belief with the themes of **rituals** and **ethics** , since doctrine influences prayer, conduct, community, and obedience.


### Belief in the Last Day: akhirah


*Akhirah* means the hereafter. Islamic teaching holds that human beings will be resurrected, judged, and held accountable. The Qur'an repeatedly discusses resurrection, the weighing or presentation of deeds, paradise, and punishment. Qur'an 99:7-8 states that even the smallest good or evil will be seen.


This doctrine answers **“Where are we going?”** Earthly death is not understood as the end of personal existence. Human life moves toward judgment and an enduring consequence beyond death.


The Last Day also changes the meaning of the present. Choices matter because they are accountable. Yet Islamic teaching combines justice with divine mercy, so students should avoid reducing the doctrine to a simple reward system. It expresses moral seriousness, hope, repentance, and trust in God.


### Belief in divine decree: qadar


*Qadar* refers to divine measure or decree. Qur'an 54:49 states that God created everything according to a measure. The doctrine affirms God's complete knowledge and sovereignty, but it also creates one of Islamic theology's deepest questions: if God knows and governs creation, how can humans be responsible?


There is no single explanation accepted in precisely the same form by every Muslim theologian. Ash'ari Sunni theology developed the idea of *kasb* , often translated as “acquisition,” to explain how acts created within God's sovereignty can still be attributed responsibly to human agents. Maturidi theology generally places greater emphasis on meaningful human capacity while maintaining divine creation and knowledge.


Twelver Shi'a thought often expresses its position as neither absolute compulsion nor unrestricted delegation. Its emphasis on *adl* , divine justice, supports the conviction that God does not judge people unjustly. These approaches differ in formulation, but each attempts to preserve both divine sovereignty and moral responsibility.


### Sunni and Shi'a frameworks


The six-part list is especially prominent in Sunni teaching. Shi'a Muslims broadly share belief in God, angels, revelation, prophets, judgment, and divine sovereignty, but Twelver Shi'a theology is often organized through five **roots of religion** , or *usul al-din* :


- *Tawhid* , divine unity
- *Adl* , divine justice
- *Nubuwwah* , prophethood
- *Imamah* , divinely guided leadership after Muhammad
- *Qiyamah* , resurrection and judgment


This is not simply a shorter version of the Sunni list. It is a different theological framework, particularly because it gives explicit prominence to divine justice and the Imamate. IB students should therefore write “in many Sunni formulations” or “in Twelver Shi'a teaching” when a distinction matters. Treating Islam as internally uniform is one of the problems explored in RevisionDojo's guide to[IB World Religions misconceptions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/ib-world-religions-misconceptions) .


### Connecting the beliefs to the five themes


The articles become easier to analyze when mapped across the course themes:


- **Rituals:** Belief in God and revelation gives worship its purpose and authority.
- **Sacred texts:** The Qur'an records teachings about God, prophets, angels, judgment, and decree.
- **Doctrines and beliefs:** The six articles form a connected account of reality and human destiny.
- **Religious experience:** Prayer, recitation, repentance, and trust may be interpreted through awareness of God and the unseen.
- **Ethics and moral conduct:** Judgment and human accountability give choices lasting significance.


This framework prevents descriptive answers from becoming six disconnected definitions. Before writing, ask which fundamental question and which theme the evidence illuminates. You can then use the[World Religions Questionbank](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/questionbank) to practise turning knowledge into comparison and evaluation.


### A practical IB revision method


Create one card for each article with four fields: Arabic term, definition, primary-text reference, and thematic connection. Then add one comparative card covering Sunni and Twelver Shi'a frameworks. Flashcards establish recall, but exam readiness comes from explaining relationships.


RevisionDojo is the ultimate IB resource for building that progression. Its Study Notes and Flashcards support knowledge, while AI Chat can test distinctions such as *qadar* and free will. The Questionbank, Grading tools, Predicted Papers, and Mock Exams help develop written responses. For longer investigations, the Coursework Library and Tutors can support source selection and argument structure. Students new to the subject can also consult[what to expect in first-term IB World Religions](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/first-term-ib-world-religions) .


### From memorising beliefs to understanding a worldview


The six articles offer a compact map of Islamic belief. God is the source of reality and guidance; angels serve within the unseen order; books communicate revelation; prophets convey it; the Last Day establishes accountability; and divine decree places existence within God's knowledge and sovereignty.


A list can be memorised in minutes. Understanding the connections takes longer, but that is where IB analysis begins. RevisionDojo helps students move from accurate terminology to careful comparison, textual evidence, and arguments that respect the diversity within Islam.
